opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the big thing for a lab like OpenMed is that they have really deep domain expertise. They know what good clinical reasoning looks like, they know where the models fall down, they have access to the right evaluators and the right kinds of data. What they usually don't want to do is build an entire RL training stack from scratch, manage a big GPU cluster, and debug distributed infrastructure. That's a huge tax on a small, focused team.

So the way we think about it is: let domain experts focus on the parts that only they can do, which is mostly defining the environment. What's the task? What does success look like? How do you grade a response? In medicine that's really subtle. It's not just "did you get the right diagnosis," it's "did you reason safely, did you hedge appropriately, did you ask for the right follow-up information, did you avoid recommending something harmful." Encoding that into a reward signal or a rubric is where the real value is, and that's where their expertise matters most.

Then our job is to make everything downstream of that as easy as possible. You write an environment, it plugs into a standard interface, and you can run evals on it, do RL against it, share it on the hub, compose it with other environments, all without rebuilding plumbing. Because the environment is the shared abstraction, the same thing you use to measure a model is the thing you use to train it. That loop is really powerful for a field like medicine, where you need to be confident in what you're measuring before you optimize against it.

The other piece is openness. A lot of medical AI work happens in silos, and I think there's a lot of value in having open environments and open models that other researchers, hospitals, and regulators can inspect and build on. If someone publishes a good clinical reasoning environment, the next group shouldn't have to reinvent it. They should be able to pick it up, train against it, and push the frontier a little further. That kind of compounding is what we're trying to enable: smaller, specialized labs getting frontier-level post-training capabilities without needing frontier-level infrastructure teams.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I'd frame it is that a lab like OpenMed has deep domain expertise. They know what good clinical reasoning looks like, they know where models fail on medical questions, and they know what a useful evaluation actually is. What they usually don't have is a team of infrastructure engineers who want to spend six months building a distributed RL training stack and wrangling compute. That gap is what we try to close.

So the first piece is compute. Medical labs often can't get reliable access to large GPU clusters on reasonable terms, and when they can, they're locked into one provider. We aggregate capacity across many providers, so you can spin up what you need, when you need it, at a price that doesn't require a big enterprise contract.

The second piece, and honestly the one I care about most, is the training stack. With verifiers and the environments hub, you can take a medical task, whether that's a diagnostic reasoning benchmark, a question-answering set, or something agentic like navigating a patient record, wrap it as an environment with a reward function, and run reinforcement learning against it on an open model. You don't have to write the async RL loop or figure out how to shard a 70B model. You write the environment, which is the part where your medical expertise actually matters, and the rest is handled.

The third piece is openness. Everything OpenMed trains, they own. The weights, the data, the environments. For medicine specifically, that matters a lot. You want to be able to audit what the model learned, you want to be able to share results with the research community, and you don't want your core capability sitting behind someone else's API that can change pricing or behavior next quarter.

And finally there's the community aspect. If OpenMed publishes a medical environment to the hub, other groups can build on it, evaluate against it, and contribute back. That compounds in a way that closed efforts just don't. My hope is that the best medical models end up being open ones, and that happens because domain experts can train them without needing to become infra experts first.
